title: Where does Back take you?
hook: Back, then a new page. Where does Back take you now?

knows: visiting web pages and pressing Back
putting things on a pile and taking the top one off
doesNotKnow: that visiting a page after going back discards the forward pages

misconception: Back always returns to the page you looked at just before, retracing the order you visited them.
objective: The learner can explain that browser history behaves like a stack: Back steps down the pile, and visiting a new page after going back throws away the pages above, so after A, B, C, Back once and D, Back lands on B.

claims.text: After visiting A, B, C, pressing Back once, visiting D and pressing Back once more, you are on B.
claims.source: Stack model: Back moves down one entry (A, B, C -> on B); visiting D from B discards everything above B (C), giving A, B, D; Back from D goes to B. Revision v4: the question was shortened from two Backs to one so the stage can reach it with one press per control. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 14): Own trace: A,B,C at C; Back -> B; visit D drops C -> A,B,D; Back -> B. Demo.tsx back()/visit() do exactly this; reveal says the same. Real browsers agree: WHATWG HTML session history, navigating removes the forward entries.

claims.text: After going back, the later pages stay in the pile, marked ahead, until you visit a new page, which throws them away.
claims.source: Unchanged text; stage behaviour in Demo.tsx visit(): pages after the current one are dropped. Revision v4 (START is now A, B, C). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 14): WHATWG HTML Living Standard, session history: on navigation, entries after the current one are removed; until then they remain (forward). Demo.tsx visit() drops pages.slice(at + 1); pages with i > at are tagged 'ahead'.

claims.text: A pile where the last page added is the first one you get back is called a stack (last in, first out).
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., 10.1 'Stacks and queues': a stack implements a last-in, first-out policy; a queue implements first-in, first-out. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): Definition: a stack is last-in, first-out (CLRS 3rd ed. 10.1, first paragraph; not opened, network blocked). Reveal wording matches.

claims.text: The stage models history as one pile and has no Forward button; it marks pages above the current page as ahead and the page just below it as where Back goes.
claims.source: Unchanged text; Demo.tsx draws 'ahead' for i > at and 'Back goes here' for i = at - 1. Revision v4. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 14): Demo.tsx: one pages array, only Back / Visit / Start over controls (no Forward); tag 'ahead' for i > at, 'Back goes here' for i = at - 1 when unlocked.

claims.text: A list of every page you opened (A, B, C, D) would put C just before D, but pressing Back from D goes to B.
claims.source: Opening order A, B, C, then D after Back; the list's entry before D is C. The history pile after visiting D from B is A, B, D (c1), so Back goes to B. Replaces the earlier closing line, which contrasted two rules that agree on this example (learner r3 N1).

recall.question: You read pages P, Q, R. You press Back once (to Q) and open a new page S. Which pages can Back and Forward now reach?
options: Back to Q and P; R is gone
Back to R, Q and P
Forward to R, back to Q and P
recall.why: History is a stack. Opening S from Q throws away R, which was above Q, and puts S on top: the pile is P, Q, S.
